summary: Reviews password-authenticated key agreement (PAKE) schemes, which let two parties use a weak shared password to authenticate each other and derive strong cryptographic keys. It describes the different kinds of schemes and gives requirements and recommendations for designers of new ones. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: A password-authenticated key exchange lets two parties who already share a password agree on a strong encryption key without ever sending the password across the network. This document sorts the kinds of scheme that exist, explains what security means for them, and lists the requirements a new scheme has to meet.

questions: how do pake schemes prevent offline attacks
what should a pake scheme document
subtitle: What a designer of a password-based key exchange has to get right, and what it has to explain.

tldr.problem: Passwords are what people use to get into things, and they are weak secrets. Protocols that prove knowledge of a password by sending something derived from it let anyone who records the exchange check a whole word list against it offline.
tldr.mechanism: A Password-Authenticated Key Exchange lets two parties prove they share a password and derive a strong key without ever putting the password or anything derived from it on the wire.
tldr.outcome: The result is a set of requirements for new schemes: they must say whether they are balanced or augmented, should come with a security proof and a constant-time implementation, and should address mapping, privacy and performance.

today: RFC 8125 is an Informational document published in April 2017 as a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group of the IRTF. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it requires no IANA actions.

sections.title: What a PAKE Is For
sections.content:
Passwords are the predominant method of accessing the Internet today, due in large part to their intuitiveness and ease of use. A user has to enter passwords repeatedly in many connections and applications, so these passwords tend to be easy to remember and can be entered repeatedly with a low probability of error. They also tend to be low-grade and not-so-random secrets that are susceptible to brute-force guessing attacks.

A Password-Authenticated Key Exchange attempts to address this by constructing a cryptographic key exchange that does not result in the password, or password-derived data, being transmitted across an unsecured channel. Two parties in the exchange prove possession of the shared password without revealing it, so such exchanges are resistant to offline, brute-force dictionary attacks. The idea was initially described by Bellovin and Merritt and has received considerable cryptographic attention since then.

PAKEs are especially interesting because they can achieve mutual authentication without requiring any Public Key Infrastructure. This document reviews different types of PAKE scheme, defines requirements for new schemes and gives additional recommendations to designers. The requirements represent the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem with passwords is not only that people choose weak ones, but that the usual way of checking one puts a hint on the wire that an attacker can take away and test at leisure. A PAKE holds the check and the key agreement together, so the hint never leaves the machine.

sections.title: The Taxonomy: Balanced, Augmented and How Keys Travel
sections.content:
Storage of the password. When both sides of a PAKE store the same representation of the password, the PAKE is said to be balanced. In a balanced PAKE the password can be stored directly in a salted state by hashing it with a random salt, or by representing the credential as an element in a finite field, for instance by multiplying a generator from a finite field by the password represented as a number to produce a password element. The benefit is that these schemes apply where either party can initiate the exchange, or both can initiate simultaneously, so that both believe themselves to be the initiator. They can be useful for mesh networking or Internet of Things applications.

When one side maintains a transform of the password and the other maintains the raw password, the PAKE is said to be augmented. Typically a client maintains the raw password, or a representation of it as in the balanced case, and a server maintains a transformed element generated with a one-way function. The benefit is some protection for the server's password that a balanced PAKE cannot give: an adversary who obtains the server's PAKE credentials cannot directly use them to impersonate the users to other servers, because the adversary would have to learn the individual passwords first, for instance by performing an offline dictionary attack. Such a scheme suits strict client-server protocols.

Transmission of public keys. All known PAKEs use public key cryptography, and a fundamental difference is how the public key is communicated. One class uses symmetric key cryptography, with a key derived from the password, to encrypt an ephemeral public key; the peer's ability to show that it decrypted the public key proves knowledge of the shared password. The first PAKE, called the Encrypted Key Exchange, works this way. Another class transmits unencrypted public keys. J-PAKE, Password Authenticated Key Exchange by Juggling, exchanges ephemeral public keys and values derived using the shared password, and if the passwords match both parties can compute a common secret by combining password, public keys and private keys. SPEKE, Strong Password-Only Authenticated Key Exchange, exchanges Diffie-Hellman values, where the generator for the public keys is derived from the shared secret, so that only the public values are exchanged and the generator is kept secret. In both cases the values transmitted across the unsecured medium are elements in a finite field and not a random blob. A combination of EKE and SPEKE is used in PACE, which is used in international travel documents; in that method a nonce is encrypted rather than a key, the nonce generates a common base for the key agreement, and without knowing the password the nonce cannot be determined, so the key agreement will fail.

Two party versus multiparty. The majority of PAKE protocols allow two parties to agree on a shared key. Proposals also exist that allow key agreement for more than two parties, called Group PAKEs or GPAKEs, and generic constructions that transform any two-party PAKE into a GPAKE. Another way to define a multiparty PAKE is to assume a trusted server with which each party shares a password; this server enables different parties to agree on a common secret key without the need to share a password among themselves, since each party has only a shared secret with the trusted server.
sections.plainLanguage: Schemes differ in three ways. They differ in what each side keeps: the same thing on both sides, or the raw password on one side and a scrambled version on the other. They differ in how the public keys travel, encrypted under a key derived from the password or in the clear. And they differ in how many people take part, two or a group.

sections.title: What Security Means for a PAKE
sections.content:
PAKE schemes are modelled on the scenario of two parties, typically Alice and Bob, who share a password, or where Bob shares a function of the password, and who would like to use it to establish a secure session key over an untrusted link. There is a powerful adversary, typically Eve, who would like to subvert the exchange. Eve has access to a dictionary that is likely to contain Alice and Bob's password, and Eve is capable of enumerating through the dictionary in a brute-force manner to try to discover it.

All PAKEs have a limitation. If Eve guesses the password, she can subvert the exchange. It is therefore necessary to model the likelihood of her discovering the password to assess the security of a PAKE. If the probability of her discovering the password is a function of interaction with the protocol participants and not a function of computation, then the PAKE is secure: Eve is unable to take information from a passive attack or from a single active attack. She cannot enumerate through her dictionary without interacting with Alice or Bob for each password guess, so the only attack left is repeated guessing. Eve learns one thing from a single active attack: whether her single guess is correct or not.

In other words, the security of a PAKE scheme rests on the idea that Eve, trying to impersonate Alice, cannot efficiently verify a password guess without interacting with Bob, or with Alice, and if she does interact she is thereby detected. It is therefore important to balance restricting the number of allowed authentication attempts against the potential of a denial-of-service vulnerability. To judge and compare schemes, security proofs in commonly accepted models SHOULD be used, and each proof and model is based on assumptions; often such proofs show that if an adversary is able to break the scheme, the adversary is also able to solve a problem assumed to be hard, such as computing a discrete logarithm, and by conversion breaking the scheme is considered to be a hard problem as well.

A PAKE scheme SHOULD be accompanied by a security proof with clearly stated assumptions and models. The proof MUST show that the probability is negligible that an active adversary would be able to pass authentication, learn additional information about the password, or learn anything about the established key. The authors MAY specify which underlying primitives are to be used with the scheme, and MAY consider specific use cases or assumptions such as resistance to quantum computers. A clear and comprehensive proof is the foundation for users to trust in the security of the scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The security of these schemes rests on one rule: an attacker cannot test a password guess without talking to the other party, and talking to them means they can see it. So the attacker learns only whether one guess was right. The number of guesses allowed has to be limited, but limiting it too far opens the door to locking the real user out, and the document wants a written proof in a stated model as the basis for trusting a scheme.

sections.title: Implementation and Elliptic Curves
sections.content:
Aside from the theoretical security of a scheme, practical implementation pitfalls have to be considered. If not carefully implemented, even a scheme that is secure in a well-defined mathematical model can leak information via side channels. The design of the scheme might allow or prevent easy protection against information leakage. In a network scenario an adversary can measure the time that the computation of an answer takes and derive information about secret parameters of the scheme. If a device operates in a potentially hostile environment, such as a smart card, other side channels like power consumption and electromagnetic emanations, or even active implementation attacks, have to be taken into account as well.

The developers of a scheme SHOULD keep the implementation aspects in mind and show how to implement the protocol in constant time. Adding a discussion about how to protect implementations of the scheme in potential hostile environments is encouraged.

Elliptic curve cryptography allows a smaller key length compared with traditional schemes based on the discrete logarithm problem in finite fields at similar security levels, so using it for PAKE schemes is also of interest. In contrast to schemes that can use the finite field element directly, an additional challenge has to be considered for some schemes based on elliptic curves, namely the mapping of a random string to an element that can be computed with, that is, a point on the curve. In some cases the opposite is needed too, the mapping of a curve point to a string that is not distinguishable from a random one. When choosing a mapping it is crucial to consider the implementation aspects as well. If the PAKE scheme is intended to be used with elliptic curves, the authors SHOULD state whether a mapping function is needed and, if so, discuss its requirements; alternatively, the authors MAY define a mapping to be used with the scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: A scheme that is sound on paper can still leak if the code takes a different amount of time depending on the secret. The document asks for constant-time implementations and a note on protecting the code in a hostile device such as a smart card. Elliptic curves need one more thing: a way to turn the password, which is a string, into a point on the curve, and getting that mapping right matters for the timing as well.

sections.title: Applications, Privacy and Performance
sections.content:
In most cases the PAKE scheme is a building block in a more complex protocol such as IPsec or TLS, which can influence the choice of a suitable scheme. An augmented scheme can be beneficial for protocols that have a strict server-client relationship; if both parties can initiate a connection, a balanced PAKE might be more appropriate.

A special variation of the network password problem is called Password-Authenticated Key Distribution, defined in an IEEE standard as password-authenticated key retrieval: the retrieval of a key from a secure key repository or escrow requiring authentication derived in part from a password. In addition to key retrieval from escrow, there is also the variant of two parties exchanging public keys using a PAKE in place of certificates. In that variant public keys can be encrypted using a password; authentication key distribution can be performed because each side knows the private key associated with its unencrypted public key and can also decrypt the peer's public key. This technique can be used to transform a short, one-time code into a long-term public key. Another possible variant allows combining authentication with certificates and the use of passwords, where the private key of the certificate is used to blind the password key agreement and the message is unblinded with the public key for verification, so a correct key establishment implies possession of the private key belonging to the certificate; this enables one-sided authentication as well as mutual authentication when the password is used. The authors MAY discuss variations of their scheme and explain application scenarios where they are beneficial, and techniques that allow long-term public key agreement are encouraged.

On privacy, each party of the PAKE protocol needs to know the identity of its communication partner in order to identify the right password for the agreement. Where a user wants a secure channel with a server, the user first has to let the server know which password to use by sending some kind of identifier. If that identifier is not protected, everyone able to eavesdrop on the connection can identify the user. To prevent this, the scheme might provide a way to protect the transmission of the user's identity, and a simple way is to use a public key provided by the server to encrypt the user's identity. The scheme MAY discuss special ideas and solutions about how to protect the privacy of the users of the scheme.

On performance, the performance of a scheme can be judged along different lines depending on the optimization goals of the target application. Potential metrics include latency, code size and area, power consumption, or exchanged messages. There might be application scenarios in which a constrained client communicates with a powerful server, in which case the scheme has to require minimal effort on the client side, and for some clients the computations might even be carried out in a hardware implementation, which requires different optimizations compared with software. The design of the scheme can also influence the cost of protecting the implementation from adversaries exploiting its physical properties. The authors MAY discuss their design choices and the influence of those choices on performance, and in particular the optimization goals could be stated.
sections.plainLanguage: Which scheme to pick depends on the protocol it is used in: a strict client and server suits the augmented kind, and a protocol where either side can start suits the balanced kind. The document also asks about the user's privacy, because the exchange usually starts with a name that identifies the user, and about performance, because the client may be a tiny battery-powered device that needs to do very little work.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The document summarizes the requirements for PAKE schemes to be compliant with it, based on the properties discussed earlier.

  • REQ1: A PAKE scheme MUST clearly state its features regarding balanced and augmented versions.
  • REQ2: A PAKE scheme SHOULD come with a security proof and clearly state its assumptions and models.
  • REQ3: The authors SHOULD show how to protect their PAKE scheme implementation in hostile environments, particularly how to implement their scheme in constant time to prevent timing attacks.
  • REQ4: If the PAKE scheme is intended to be used with elliptic curves, the authors SHOULD discuss their requirements for a potential mapping or define a mapping to be used with the scheme.
  • REQ5: The authors of a PAKE scheme MAY discuss its design choice with regard to performance, that is, its optimization goals.
  • REQ6: The authors of a scheme MAY discuss variations of their scheme that allow use in special application scenarios; in particular, techniques that facilitate long-term public key agreement are encouraged.
  • REQ7: Authors of a scheme MAY discuss special ideas and solutions on privacy protection of its users.
  • REQ8: The authors MUST follow the IRTF IPR policy.

The IANA considerations section says the document requires no IANA actions, and the security considerations section says the document analyses requirements for a cryptographic scheme, with security considerations discussed throughout.
sections.plainLanguage: In short, a scheme must say whether it is balanced or augmented and must follow the research group's patent policy. It should come with a security proof, with a constant-time implementation, and, if it uses elliptic curves, with a mapping. It may discuss performance, variations for particular uses and the privacy of its users.

items.title: A guess needs interaction
items.text: An attacker cannot check a password guess without talking to the other party, and talking means being seen.

items.title: One bit per attempt
items.text: From a single active attack the attacker learns only whether that one guess was correct.

items.title: Attempts must be limited
items.text: The number of allowed authentication attempts has to be balanced against the risk of denial of service.

items.title: A written proof
items.text: The scheme should come with a proof in a stated model, showing that an active adversary has only a negligible chance of passing, learning about the password, or learning the key.

items.title: Implementation leaks too
items.text: Even a secure scheme can leak through timing and other side channels, so the code must run in constant time.
